sections.html:
Chicago Heights is a Cook County city about 30 miles south of the Chicago Loop, covering 10.38 square miles. Its neighbors include Homewood, Flossmoor, Park Forest, Glenwood, Sauk Village, Olympia Fields, Ford Heights and South Chicago Heights, so a seller's comparable sales often cross village lines.

The city peaked at 40,900 residents in 1970 and has lost people in every census since, reaching 27,480 in 2020, with an estimate of 26,533 for 2024. The 2020 count lists 9,261 households and 10,663 housing units, 13.1 percent of them vacant. The homeowner vacancy rate was 4.0 percent and the rental vacancy rate 13.3 percent. That is more supply than a growing suburb has, so price and condition matter a great deal to buyers.

The city charges a real estate transfer tax of $4.00 per $1,000 of sale price, and the seller is responsible for paying it. Three city offices must be cleared before the stamp is issued, and the city's instruction sheet lists the order in which to visit them.

Transfer stamp steps
StepOffice and phoneWhat happens
1Code Enforcement, 708-756-5328For-sale inspection; unpaid liens and building violations resolved
2Water Billing, 708-756-5344Final meter reading, booked at least 3 days before the loan closing; final bill
3City Clerk, 708-756-5304Other unpaid fees or citations; transfer tax payment
4Code EnforcementCertificate of Occupancy after the final inspection passes and any escrow is posted

The clerk's office needs the completed application signed by seller and buyer, a photocopy of the new deed, the Certificate of Occupancy and the state PTAX-203 declaration. Payment must be cash, money order, or a cashier's, certified, attorney or title company check. Credit cards, debit cards and personal checks are not accepted, and each payment (transfer tax, exemption fee, water, escrow) is separate.

Code Enforcement oversees property maintenance, building safety and regulatory compliance, and it conducts residential and commercial sale and rental inspections for life-safety standards. The city's codes include the 2018 International Residential Code, the 2012 Property Maintenance Code, the 2014 Illinois Plumbing Code and the 2017 National Electrical Code.

  • Call 708-756-5328 early, because the Certificate of Occupancy depends on a passed final inspection.
  • Resolve open violations or liens, or post an escrow where the city allows it.
  • Ask whether the inspection date and result affect your closing schedule.

Repairs that a for-sale inspection finds do not disappear in a cash sale. A buyer who takes the house as-is still has to satisfy the city's requirements, so ask Code Enforcement how an as-is transfer is handled before you accept an offer.

Chicago Heights runs a defaulted mortgage and foreclosure property registration program, administered by Hera Property Registry. Owners, mortgagees and trustees must register online and pay a fee.

If the house has sat empty, register it, resolve the violations and gather the permit history before listing. A buyer's attorney will ask about each,.

Illinois taxes the transfer of real estate at 50 cents per $500 of value or fraction under 35 ILCS 200/31-10, using the declaration filed in MyDec. When the deed is recorded with the Cook County Clerk, staff check for the state stamp and for any local stamp the municipality requires.

Even a quitclaim deed with no money changing hands needs stamps and an exempt-transfer notation. Chicago Heights separately charges a $100 processing fee for exempt transfers and requires an original signed, notarized deed, so a photocopy will not do.

sections.h2: What to bring to the clerk
sections.html:
• The application signed by both seller and buyer.
  • A photocopy of the new deed.
  • The Certificate of Occupancy from Code Enforcement.
  • The state PTAX-203 declaration.
  • An acceptable form of payment for each separate charge.

Missing any one of these means a second trip. Call the clerk at 708-756-5304 the day before and read the list back. If the transfer is exempt, bring the original signed, notarized deed along with the $100 processing fee.

Because the city takes only certain forms of payment, plan a trip to the bank. A cashier's check or money order for each charge keeps the counter visit short. Cash works too, but a receipt matters, so keep every one with your closing papers. Ask your title company or attorney which of the payments they will bring and which are yours.

Book the water reading first, since it has a fixed lead time of at least three days before the loan closing. The inspection and the Certificate of Occupancy come next, because the clerk will not accept the application without it.

sections.h2: How the order of offices affects your timeline
sections.html:
The steps run in sequence, so a delay at the first office pushes everything after it. If the for-sale inspection finds violations, you must resolve them or post an escrow before the Certificate of Occupancy is issued. The clerk will not issue a stamp without that certificate. Plan your closing date with room to spare, and ask your buyer whether the date can move if a repair takes longer than expected.

The water reading needs at least three days of notice before the loan closing, and the Certificate of Occupancy depends on the final inspection. Start both in the same week. Then use the days in between to gather the deed copy, the PTAX-203 and your payment forms, so the clerk visit is the last step and not another delay.

sections.h2: Listing, selling privately or taking a cash offer
sections.html:
A listing reaches the most buyers, but the city's inspection and stamp process falls on the seller either way. Selling privately saves a commission and puts the paperwork on you. A cash offer on an as-is house can shorten the timeline, particularly when the house has open violations, a vacancy problem or an estate behind it.

Compare the net from each route after repairs, carrying costs and the city's fees, and ask each buyer how they will handle the for-sale inspection.

sections.h2: What to ask a buyer before you sign
sections.html:
• Who orders and pays for the for-sale inspection, and who fixes what it finds?
  • Who pays the $4.00 per $1,000 tax? The city holds the seller responsible, so a contract that shifts it should say so plainly.
  • Will the buyer close on a date that leaves time for the water reading and the Certificate of Occupancy?
  • If there is an escrow for open items, who posts it?

Get those answers in writing before you sign anything. A written list of duties keeps both sides clear when the clerk's counter asks for a document.

faqs.q: Who pays the Chicago Heights transfer tax?
faqs.a: The seller. The city's rate is $4.00 per $1,000 of sale price, and it is paid at the City Clerk's office.

faqs.q: How do I pay the Chicago Heights transfer tax?
faqs.a: With cash, a money order, or a cashier's, certified, attorney or title company check. The city does not accept credit or debit cards or personal checks.

faqs.q: When should I schedule the final water reading?
faqs.a: At least three days before the loan closing. Call Water Billing at 708-756-5344.

faqs.q: Do I need an inspection to sell in Chicago Heights?
faqs.a: Yes for a standard sale. Call Code Enforcement at 708-756-5328 to schedule a for-sale inspection and to clear unpaid violations or liens. Exempt transfers may need a check on whether an inspection applies.

faqs.q: What does an exempt transfer cost?
faqs.a: The city charges a $100 processing fee for an exempt stamp. The original notarized deed is required and no photocopy is accepted.
